title: Quantum Computing-The Underlying Principle Behind it
abstract_summary: This review presents the fundamentals of quantum computing—qubits, superposition, entanglement and coherence—along with historical milestones and core algorithms (Shor, Grover, Deutsch–Jozsa), and examines hardware approaches and error correction challenges. It surveys applications across healthcare, finance (fraud detection, risk management, credit scoring), cryptography, materials science and quantum networking, and discusses limitations, future prospects and the need for post-quantum cryptographic solutions.
methodology_description: This work is a non-empirical narrative literature review and conceptual overview of quantum computing and its relevance to multiple application domains (including financial services). The authors synthesized published literature (books, review articles, conference proceedings, journal articles and preprints) to: (1) outline historical development and a timeline of quantum computing, (2) describe core physical principles (superposition, entanglement, coherence) and qubit/gate representations (Bloch sphere, common gates), (3) summarize prominent quantum algorithms (Shor, Grover, Deutsch–Jozsa, QPE, VQE, QAOA, amplitude estimation, etc.), (4) survey application areas (healthcare, finance, cryptography, AI/ML, materials science) and (5) enumerate limitations and research challenges (decoherence, scalability, error correction, hardware and software barriers). The review uses cited primary and secondary sources across the quantum computing literature to support statements and to point to example industry roadmaps (IBM, Google, Microsoft) and experimental milestones (satellite QKD, teleportation). The authors did not report original experiments, simulations, or empirical evaluation; instead they compiled and interpreted existing results and projections. The manuscript also discloses use of generative AI for language polishing; all substantive content and references were curated from the literature and edited by the authors.
key_findings: [speculative] Quantum computers leverage superposition, entanglement and coherence to enable parallel exploration of multiple states and (in some cases) large reductions in computation time.
[speculative] Shor's algorithm gives exponential speedup for integer factorization compared with the best-known classical algorithms.
[speculative] Grover's algorithm offers a quadratic speedup for unstructured database search (O(√N) vs O(N)).
[speculative] The Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm solves the constant-vs-balanced oracle problem with an exponential advantage over naïve classical evaluation.
[supported] Long-distance satellite-based quantum entanglement distribution has been demonstrated (references to Micius experiments with entanglement/teleportation beyond 1,200 km).
[supported] Experimental progress in quantum error correction and decoding has been reported (paper cites Bausch et al. 2024 showing improved error decoding performance on Google hardware).

[speculative] Roadmaps from major vendors (IBM, Microsoft) foresee rapid qubit-count growth and new qubit types (e.g., IBM 'Flamingo' and 'Kookaburra' processors, Microsoft 'Majorana 1' topological-qubit efforts), with potential to improve scalability and stability.

[supported] Leading qubit platforms (superconducting, trapped-ion) currently exhibit coherence times typically in the microsecond-to-millisecond range, requiring cryogenics and shielding to maintain operations.
[supported] Quantum error correction (QEC) imposes very large resource overheads (many physical qubits per logical qubit); achieving fault tolerance remains the central engineering challenge.
[speculative] Practical, large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers will likely require millions of high-quality qubits and dramatic reductions in physical error rates.
[supported] Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and related protocols rely on quantum principles (e.g., no-cloning) and have been demonstrated in satellite and metropolitan fibre testbeds.

[speculative] Quantum algorithms and subroutines (e.g., amplitude estimation, QAOA, VQE) are promising for finance use-cases such as Value-at-Risk (VaR) estimation, portfolio optimization and Monte Carlo acceleration.
[speculative] Amplitude estimation offers a quadratic speedup for certain Monte Carlo–style estimation tasks compared with classical Monte Carlo methods (in algorithmic theory).
[speculative] Hybrid quantum–classical approaches (variational algorithms, ML-assisted workflows) are a near-term practical strategy given current NISQ hardware limitations.

[supported] Major financial institutions and technology companies are actively exploring quantum computing for fraud detection, risk management and optimization (the paper cites industry interest and pilot efforts).
[supported] Current quantum hardware is costly to build and operate (cryogenics, vacuum, precision control) and access is mostly concentrated among well-funded labs, vendors and cloud providers.
[speculative] Quantum computing could transform domains such as drug discovery, materials modelling, climate and energy modelling if scalable fault-tolerant machines become available.
[supported] Quantum software ecosystems and programming tools are immature relative to classical stacks; algorithm discovery, verification and error-mitigation remain active research problems.
results_summary: This review summarizes quantum-computing principles (superposition, entanglement, coherence), canonical algorithms (Shor, Grover, Deutsch–Jozsa), hardware progress (superconducting, trapped-ion, topological research), and the principal barriers to practical deployment (decoherence, error correction overhead, scalability, cost). It highlights experimentally demonstrated advances including satellite QKD and recent error-decoding improvements, and it emphasizes the potential relevance of quantum algorithms to finance (VaR, portfolio optimization, fraud detection) primarily as theoretical or early-stage pilot possibilities rather than production-ready capabilities.
performance_claims: Satellite quantum teleportation / entanglement distribution demonstrated beyond 1,200 kilometres (Yin et al., 2017).
IBM roadmap items cited: 'Flamingo' (1,386 qubits) and 'Kookaburra' (4,158 qubits) (paper cites AbuGhanem, 2025).
Google 'Willow' chip reported learning-based error decoding results and performance improvements crossing an error-correction threshold (Bausch et al., 2024).
Typical coherence times for present qubit platforms cited as microseconds to milliseconds (paper statement).
Quantum error correction resource claim: thousands of physical qubits required to encode one logical qubit (paper statement / consensus estimate).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper presents algorithmic proofs and established theoretical speedups (e.g., Shor, Grover, amplitude estimation) and cites experimental milestones in specialized demonstrations (QKD, error-decoding advances). However, no broad, empirical quantum advantage for practical financial workloads is demonstrated; claims about large-scale speedups or disruptive production use in finance remain theoretical or at pilot stage.
limitations: Qubit instability and decoherence: qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise (temperature variations, EM noise, vibrations) leading to short coherence times (micro- to milliseconds) that limit circuit depth and computation length.

Scalability and system complexity: scaling to the millions of high-quality qubits required for practical applications is hindered by connectivity, cross-talk, physical footprint, cooling and control infrastructure.

Error rates, error correction overhead and lack of fault tolerance: current gate and decoherence error rates are too high; quantum error correction (QEC) requires thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit, imposing massive resource overhead.

Hardware limitations and manufacturing challenges: need for specialized equipment (cryogenics, ultra-high vacuum, precision control electronics), advanced materials and fabrication techniques; qubit consistency and yield at scale remain unresolved.

Diversity of competing qubit technologies without a clear winner: superconducting qubits, trapped ions, photonic and topological approaches each have trade-offs and no consensus on which will enable large-scale fault-tolerant machines.

Immature software, algorithms and toolchains: few practical quantum algorithms for real-world problems (especially finance) and nascent programming languages, tooling and verification methods; programming often requires low-level hardware knowledge.
Probabilistic nature and verification difficulty: the inherent probabilistic outputs and quantum state collapse complicate correctness, reproducibility and verification of results.
Cryptographic threats: large-scale quantum computers would break widely used public-key schemes (RSA, ECC), creating urgent security risks and migration challenges to post-quantum cryptography.

Financial and accessibility barriers: very high capital and operational costs restrict access to large-scale quantum hardware to elite institutions; cloud offerings are limited in qubit count and stability.
Quantum networking challenges: photon loss, need for quantum repeaters, and reliable long-distance entanglement distribution remain significant obstacles to building a practical quantum internet.
Central challenge of QEC emphasized as the main barrier: achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation is currently impractical with present technology and error rates.

contradictions: The paper accepts theoretical quantum advantages (Shor, Grover, amplitude estimation) while simultaneously emphasising that practical advantage for finance is unlikely in the near term due to noise, QEC overhead and qubit requirements—creating a tension between algorithmic promises and practical feasibility.

It cites vendor roadmaps that forecast substantial qubit-count growth (e.g., IBM 'Flamingo'/'Kookaburra') but also stresses that fault-tolerant, large-scale machines will likely require millions of qubits; this highlights a contradiction/tension between optimistic vendor timelines and the paper's realistic assessment of scalability challenges.
